title: 10 Reasons for Public Executions

There was no public demand that led to the U.S. military announcing that it would publicly execute someone on livestreamed video (a list of advertisers, if any, during the broadcast has not been released — add your guesses below). No polling favored it. No fashion for being like Saudi Arabia was afloat. Outside of Supreme Court Justices, a return to the 18th century is generally not in vogue. So why do it? I can guess at a few contributing factors.







They can probably do it. They can’t take over countries. They can’t steal Iran’s oil. They can’t make Greenland a state. They can’t end or make anyone like their wars in Palestine or Ukraine. title: Reactors on the Moon?
content:
Endangerment, Environment, North America, Why End War, World

By Karl Grossman, CounterPunch, October 9, 2026

The lead front page story in the New York Times this week was headlined: “Superpowers Racing to Put Nuclear Reactors on Moon.” The nations involved: the U.S., China and Russia. And there was a subhead: “Experts Warn of Radioactive Risks From a Rocket Mishap or Lunar Meltdown.”

The reporter, Selam Gebrekidan, wrote: “Failures could cause a chain reaction with dire consequences. Falling reactor debris could scatter radioactive material….An explosion or a meltdown on the moon’s surface could risk turning entire regions into no-go zones.”

The extensive story quoted Edward Lyman, director of nuclear power safety at the Union of Concerned Scientists, saying: “There will always be a space race going on, and if you enter nuclear power into that mix, then it could take a potentially more dangerous turn.”

Nuclear power and weapons in space have been an unexpectedly extensive part of my journalistic journey. Because of having been deeply involved in reporting about the plans of the Long Island Lighting Company to construct seven to 11 nuclear power plants on Long Island, where I live, I became knowledgeable about atomic energy.

I wrote a book titled “Power Crazy” about this scheme to turn the island into what nuclear promoters termed then a “nuclear park.” I wrote many column

The latest news is of war fighting around the nuclear facilities in Zaporizhzhya, Ukraine. When Russia first invaded, unarmed civilians protected the dangerous site in Zaporizhzhya, but as soon as armed troops took over, the shooting started, and it’s worsened since, with taboos being tossed aside in succession as if the continued existence of humanity is grounds for not only keeping nuclear weapons and power plants around but also for upping the risks just a little.




The largest nuclear power plant in Europe, with six 1,000 MW reactors and decades’ worth of nuclear waste, is now in a battlefield. Already in this war (find a summary in 

No to Nuclear

title: Books or Bombs? France’s Student Revolt vs. NATO’s Spending Push
content:
By 

Medea Benjamin

, October 8, 2026




For the third week in a row, high school students across France are taking to the streets demanding more investment in their education. They want more teachers, smaller classes, decent school buildings and a public education system that works for poor and working-class students.




But their struggle comes at a moment when France faces mounting pressure to cut public spending while dramatically increasing its military budget. The question at the heart of this uprising goes far beyond education: Will France invest in its young people—or in missiles, weapons and war? Books or bombs?




What began in the Paris suburbs has spread to more than a thousand schools. On October 6, more than 250,000 people reportedly took to the streets in demonstrations supporting the students.




The government’s response has only deepened the anger. Instead of addressing students’ demands, authorities have unleashed riot police, tear gas, grenades and mass arrests. More than 6,500 people have reportedly been arrested since the protests began, most of them minors. Some young protesters have suffered horrific injuries, including a 15-year-old who lost his hand after a police grenade exploded. Amnesty International has condemned what it calls the “disproportionate” use of force against young people peacefully demanding their right to education.

title: Which Way Is Peace?
content:
By David Swanson, World BEYOND War, October 3, 2026




Remarks in Baltimore on October 3, 2026, at event with 

War Is Still A Lie




Thank you to Ronda Cooperstein and the local chapter of World BEYOND War for setting this event up.




I recently read a big stack of books on the decline and elimination of dueling. There were thousands of factors, many of them beyond anyone’s easy control, but key among them was cultural change, was bringing people to find greater humiliation in dueling than in not dueling, greater respect in refusing to duel than in being willing to duel. The picture of dueling as noble, respectable, and courageous was replaced by one much nearer the truth: drunken primadonnas misperceiving insults and committing murder for lack of the ability to admit they were idiots. And dueling died by stages. More and more would-be duelists’ so-called seconds negotiated peace. More and more duels ended without deaths or injuries, often with bullets intentionally shot into the air. More and more duelists were prosecuted for the crime. More and more newspaper cartoonists depicted duelists as monkeys and clowns. Dueling was outlawed and denounced for centuries before the abolitionists finally succeeded.

title: 10 Reasons to Oppose the “Arc de Trump”
content:
Culture of Peace, North America

By Medea Benjamin, September 30, 2026

There was already widespread opposition to Trump’s proposed arch at Memorial Circle in Arlington, Virginia—a 250-foot structure, roughly the height of a 20-story building and 50 percent taller than Paris’s Arc de Triomphe. Now the controversy has intensified: Trump says the arch, which originally included plans for an observation deck, a café, a gift shop and exhibition space, would also function as a military complex, housing drones, snipers and ammunition.

Here are 10 reasons (really 9 plus your own) to oppose the “Arc de Trump.”

1. It would overwhelm one of America’s most important historic landscapes. The giant arch would sit directly on the ceremonial axis connecting Arlington House, Arlington National Cemetery, Memorial Bridge and the Lincoln Memorial, dramatically altering this historic view and dwarfing the surrounding monuments rather than complementing them.

2. It clashes with the very meaning of the site. Arlington Memorial Bridge and the surrounding landscape were conceived as symbols of national reconciliation after the Civil War. And Arlington National Cemetery is a solemn resting place for hundreds of thousands of service members. title: Trump’s Offer to Sell Weapons to China Is Wonderful
content:
Asia, Demilitarization, North America, Stop Arms Trade, World

By David Swanson, World BEYOND War, September 30, 2026

Wednesday morning I was speaking by Zoom to a college class about war and peace, and one of the students asked about the risk of the U.S. demilitarizing and other nations not. I gave a standard answer about how a reverse arms race could be done in stages. The U.S. could commit to not spending more than three times any other nation on its military and proceed downward from there. Of the couple of dozen nations that spend much of anything on their militaries, all but three are U.S. allies and weapons customers being hammered hard by the U.S. government (and NATO) to spend more. The only country spending more than a tiny fraction of the U.S. — in fact, spending close to a third of U.S. military spending as it’s usually reported or a sixth of what it really is — is China. If the U.S. were to keep its nukes out of South Korea and Japan, and its troops out of South Korea, and finally end the war and turn South Korea’s military over to South Korea, and start joining treaties and courts and beginning a general disarmament, North Korea would almost certainly join in serious negotiations about getting rid of its nukes, while China would — I guaranteed to this college class — not keep increasing its own military spending.

author: David Swanson
title: One Down! Abolishing Dueling and Warmaking
content:
By David Swanson, World BEYOND War, September 29, 2026




According to an 1838 U.S.-published instruction manual for dueling, the practice of dueling was going to last “as long as a manly independence, and a lofty personal pride in all that dignifies and ennobles the human character, shall continue to exist.”[1] Be that as it may, dueling was soon gone as a practice in any way acceptable or routine, and most of the globe had never had it to begin with.




Many years ago, I wrote a book about the outlawrists of the 1920s, people (led by lawyers) who were fond of pointing out that dueling had been outlawed and abolished, and so could war be. Yet dueling had persisted for centuries in Europe and in the United States despite laws forbidding it as murder. And we’ve now gone a century with laws forbidding war, while the wars persist.




I do not doubt for a minute that laws helped end dueling. Nobody could have finally begun using the laws had there not been any. Nobody could have denounced dueling as a crime had it not been a crime. But I’ve encountered over the years numerous cursory accounts of dueling that explain its demise in very simple terms, albeit each explanation different from all the others. title: How World BEYOND War Chapters in Africa Marked International Peace Day 2026
content:
By Guy Feugap, World BEYOND War’s Africa Organizer, September 27, 2026




To mark the 2026 International Day of Peace, the African chapters of World BEYOND War organized awareness-raising activities on issues that threaten peace in their countries. In Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, The Gambia, and South Sudan, these activities also served as opportunities to mobilize support and advocate for peace.




In Cameroon, more than 5,000 people from various walks of life took part in a peace march. title: Podcast: Beyond Borders with Khawaja Hammad Akbar (#NoWar2026 Preview)
content:
Asia, Culture of Peace, Demilitarization, How I Became a Peace Activist, Myth of Necessity, Nonviolent Activism, Podcasts, World BEYOND War Podcast

By Marc Eliot Stein, September 26, 2026, World BEYOND War

“Beyond Borders” is the theme of World BEYOND War’s #NoWar2026 online conference next month. To preview this conference, I spoke with Khawaja Hammad Akbar, a peace builder in Pakistan who will be leading a panel on case studies of militarized borders and demilitarized zones with speakers from Korea, Gaza and the US/Mexico border.

What does it mean to seek a world “beyond borders”? To begin exploring this question, I asked Khawaja about his own background and motivations for antiwar work and discovered that his interest began (as it so often does) with his desire to understand his own family legacy. As we talked about the devastation and trauma left behind by the 1947 India/Pakistan partition, a familiar pattern became clear: the borders of the past still imprison all of us.

We also talked about popular attitudes about militarism in our own societies, about our hopes for a better future, and about the inspiration of past teachers of peace like Syed Ahmad Khan. The closing music is an excerpt from a live recording of “Ballot Box” by Penboy, a singer and spoken word poet who will be performing at the #NoWar2026 conference which takes place October 23, 24 and 25.

By Medea Benjamin and Nicolas J. S. Davies, World BEYOND War, September 22, 2026

The Trump administration came perilously close to launching another bombing campaign against Yemen this weekend. According to a September 20 New York Times report, US commanders had approved their targets, American troops were loading bombs onto warplanes, and an attack on Yemen’s Ansar Allah forces was about to begin when President Trump abruptly reversed course.

For two weeks, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had been pleading with Trump to intervene as Ansar Allah (Houthi) forces swept through Saudi-backed forces’ positions along Yemen’s Red Sea coast. Trump initially resisted, but after another urgent call from the Saudi crown prince, he instructed the Pentagon to prepare for airstrikes. By Sunday, he had changed his mind again, at least temporarily.

The New York Times reported that many of Trump’s closest advisers opposed joining the Saudi war. U.S. military officials also questioned whether renewed bombing would accomplish anything, given that Ansar Allah had withstood more than 1,000 U.S. strikes during a seven-week campaign in 2025. That operation consumed roughly $1 billion in munitions and other military resources in its first month alone.

title: The Cost of Arms Deals and Corruption in Cameroon
content:
Africa, Cameroon Chapter, Chapters, Economic Cost, Stop Arms Trade

By Guy Feugap, Africa Organizer for World BEYOND War, Corruption Tracker, September 13, 2026

When corruption scandals erupt in the arms trade, attention focuses on the millions embezzled, the officials implicated, and the ensuing legal proceedings. Yet the true cost of these cases often runs much deeper. Behind opaque contracts and illicit commissions lie consequences that directly affect governance, citizens’ trust in their institutions, and, above all, the security of the population. The Defex case, which brought to light corrupt practices in arms contracts between Spain and Cameroon, offers an opportunity to question a security model based on the accumulation of weapons. The Cameroonian case shows that corruption in the arms trade undermines public finances and jeopardizes human security; it thus raises a fundamental question: Can lasting peace truly be built on the foundations of militarism?

In the arms deals between Spain and Cameroon, a financial scandal has implicated high-ranking officials in the Cameroonian government, as documented by Corruption Tracker, which released the report Defex’s Dirty Decades: Arms Sales to Cameroon in September 2025.
